statement: What counts as subconscious depends on where the conscious/unconscious boundary is drawn and how awareness is measured.
Carried from TL-08: memory reactivation in sleep may stay implicit while fragments surface in dreams; anaesthesia dreaming is disconnected consciousness. The mechanism is a proposal.
Both rest on awareness thresholds and report-based classification, and in both the threshold choice changes the conclusion.

Mystical, self-transcendent and minimal-awareness states are known only through structured reports (MEQ; minimal phenomenal experience questionnaire), and the phase track's mystical-experience thread sits on the Spirit/Consciousness boundary.
Traditions describe both a reality beyond ordinary experience (Spirit) and pure or nondual awareness (Consciousness); whether these are one thing or two is a philosophical and spiritual question.
Folk beliefs about what survives death favour mental states over bodily ones, so beliefs about the soul track the mental and conscious side of the person.
The same end-of-life events are studied as soul-related experiences (end-of-life and near-death experiences) and as consciousness questions (awareness during circulatory arrest).
Death anxiety is a hypothesised meeting point: Terror Management treats soul and afterlife beliefs as defences against it (a hypothesis), and death anxiety falls after psychedelic experiences.
The track studies the Soul as belief about what persists and the Spirit as reported experience of what transcends; the distinction is the track's framework, not a finding about souls or spirits.
Soul beliefs are also measured implicitly (mind associated with 'airy' properties), using the implicit methods of the Subconscious topic.
Nearly half of end-of-life experiences occurred during sleep, where the memory theory places implicit reactivation; any link is a hypothesis.
Both rest partly on experimental effects (induced awe; behavioural priming) that failed replication.
In Yogacara and Advaita, subliminal and deep-sleep states are described within a path of realisation, the same vocabulary of realisation traditions use for mystical experience.

Traditions and history describe the subliminal as a form or degree of consciousness (descriptive). The dependence holds within these teachings, so the link is Philosophical/Spiritual; CN0-10 keeps the description Established.

During circulatory arrest, possible implicit learning (a subconscious sense) is reported alongside a possible 'spectrum of consciousness'. One feasibility study with 9 usable EEGs and 3 guesses; hence Hypothetical.
Beliefs about the topic shape moral judgment: afterlife certainty and approval of mind upload; free-will belief and punishment.
Responsibility and justice turn on judgments about minds: who is judged to act freely, and who is judged conscious.
Ego dissolution is graded with psychedelic dose and correlates with unitive mystical measures: a construct both topics measure.
The track itself filed the psychedelic death-anxiety meta-analysis (TD-SPIRIT-31) as deepening a Soul claim on beliefs about what continues after death (TC-SOUL-01).
The track filed the circulatory-arrest study (TD-CONS-29) as deepening the contested near-death hypothesis (TC-SOUL-21); the dependency is only as strong as that hypothesis.
Across traditions soul and spirit share a breath and life vocabulary (description of texts, carried from the main-report link L10).
Traditions draw the soul/spirit boundary differently; no single boundary (carried from L11).
Soul, brain process or neither as the subject of experience; near-death reports read either way (carried from L12 and L27).
Altered and mystical states may share neural signatures; criticality estimates can be inflated by non-stationary input (carried from L18).
In Jain and Advaita teaching the self is consciousness; Indian Buddhist philosophy denies an abiding self (teachings described, not shown).
Higher-order theories define the unconscious/conscious difference relationally; Tsikandilakis et al. argue automatic processes interact with awareness.

In African ethics (Gyekye) and animist traditions soul as moral personhood and spirit as connection are read together, without a doctrine of interior souls (teachings described, carried from Reports 3 and 4).
Unconscious-processing findings bear on access; whether phenomenal states without access exist is disputed (carried from L08).
